"At a time when working families are fighting tooth and nail to make ends meet while the Administration sells them out to corrupt special interests, we need to stand behind leaders who are accountable to working people and stand up to greedy corporations," Ocasio-Cortez said, according to Nixon's campaign. FLA DEM SEN-NOMINEE ANGIE NIXON BACKED ABOLISHING ELECTORAL COLLEGE, RANKED-CHOICE VOTING IN RESURFACED CLIPS "I'm honored to have the endorsement of Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and her support as we work towards a better future for Florida," Nixon said, according to her campaign. Together, we’re going to fight for everyone: working families, students, and communities who have been ignored for too long. articles.title: Convicted predators face lifetime barrier under GOP lawmaker’s sweeping victim protection bill
articles.summary: Rep. Abe Hamadeh's, R-Ariz., Kayleigh's Law passed the House unanimously, requiring lifetime no-contact orders for convicted sex crime and violent felony offenders.
articles.body: An Arizona congressman is putting convicted predators on notice after the House unanimously backed a bill designed to prevent abusers from dragging their victims back into court years after their crimes. "Protect the victim. Stop the predator. End the revolving door," Rep. Abe Hamadeh, R-Ariz., wrote on X after the House passed Kayleigh’s Law. "When a predator is convicted, the court issues a lifetime no-contact order," he added. "Not until probation ends. Not until some judge decides he’s ‘moved on.’ For life." Hamadeh told Fox News Digital that the legislation would deliver permanent protection to survivors of federal sex crimes and violent felonies by requiring courts to issue lifetime no-contact injunctions against convicted offenders. TRUMP SIGNS HAWLEY MEASURE ADDING 200 CHILD EXPLOITATION INVESTIGATORS IN LARGEST CRACKDOWN EFFORT YET "This is a common-sense type of bill where we’re supporting victims, and we’re prioritizing victims over criminals," Hamadeh said. The Kayleigh’s Law Act of 2026, introduced by Hamadeh as H.R. 8481, passed the House with unanimous support Monday and now heads to the Senate. The legislation is named after Kayleigh Kozak, an Arizona mother of five who was sexually abused as a child and later forced to return to court when her abuser sought to have a no-contact protection lifted. Hamadeh said Kozak was hauled back into court 13 years after the abuse, and then had to return again when the man made another attempt the following year. CALIFORNIA DEMS TRIGGER OUTRAGE AFTER SIDING WITH CONVICTED CHILD SEX OFFENDERS IN SHOCKING VOTE "Can you imagine that you have to sit across the room from this man?" Hamadeh said. "That’s something a victim should never have to do." The federal bill would prohibit an offender from contacting the victim directly or indirectly for the rest of the offender’s life, even after prison, probation or supervised release ends. "When you abuse a child, or you sexually abuse a child, or if you commit a violent offense against them, you should never have to interact with that person ever in their lives," Hamadeh said. Kozak’s fight for permanent protections grew out of her own experience with Joshua Jacobsen, a former teacher and soccer coach who pleaded guilty to sexual abuse and luring a minor for sexual exploitation. Kozak was 12 years old and one of his students when the abuse occurred, according to FOX 10 Phoenix. NEWSOM-BACKED LAW LETS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHILD RAPIST SEEK EARLY RELEASE AGAIN AS DA URGES 'STOP THE MADNESS' Jacobsen was sentenced to six months in jail and lifetime probation. Nearly two decades later, he asked a Maricopa County judge to end that probation, arguing that his conduct over the previous 18 years showed he had reformed and was ready to "move on," the outlet reported. Kozak returned to court to oppose his request. "I am living proof that he is capable of sexually harming children," Kozak told the court. "He consciously chose to violate me, and he was convicted of committing a dangerous crime against a child while he was in a position of power." Jacobsen’s effort ultimately failed. A Maricopa County judge denied his request in June, citing probation violations that included unauthorized contact with children and breaches of chaperone restrictions, according to Arizona’s Family. Jacobsen remains on lifetime probation under the supervision of Maricopa County Adult Probation. Kozak celebrated the House vote on X, saying the country was "one step closer" to giving victims of heinous crimes the permanent protection they deserve. PREP SCHOOL TEACHER FILMED SEX WITH STUDENT SHE WAS TUTORING: ‘NOT MY BEST THINKING’ "No victim should ever have to endure the hell I had to walk through," she wrote. "When I discovered protection wasn’t permanent, I knew it had to change." Versions of Kayleigh’s Law have passed in Arizona and Wisconsin. Hamadeh said more than 1,000 Arizona survivors secured lifetime protection during the state law’s first year. In a statement announcing the House vote, Hamadeh’s office said the legislation aims to end the "legal tug-of-war" that forces survivors to repeatedly face their attackers in court to maintain basic protections. "Victims should never again have to fill out another form, sit across from their abuser, or look over their shoulder because the sentence ran out, and the system shrugged," Hamadeh said in a statement following the vote. The issue became personal for Hamadeh long before he entered Congress. SENATOR TIM SHEEHY: SOFT-ON-CRIME JUDGES NEED CONSEQUENCES. THE JAIL ACT DELIVERS He met Kozak about five years ago while running for Arizona attorney general. Years later, as he campaigned for Congress, the two met outside an In-N-Out Burger, where he made her a promise. "I told Kayleigh, I said, ‘Kayleigh, the moment I get to Congress, it’s going to be one of my first bills that I get done,’" Hamadeh recalled. Kozak and her children later joined Hamadeh at the Capitol as the House approved the legislation. "Promise made, promise kept," Hamadeh said. "To actually see it done has been really wonderful." Hamadeh, a former prosecutor and Army veteran, said Kozak transformed the trauma she endured into a campaign that could protect millions of other survivors. NEW YORK BILLS COULD ABOLISH LIFE WITHOUT PAROLE FOR SERIAL KILLERS AND COP KILLERS, CRITICS WARN "She’s turned this tragedy into something that’s an inspiration to so many," he said. "From the moment it happened, it’s always been personal to me." Asked about defendants’ due process rights, Hamadeh noted that the restrictions would apply only after a conviction. "This is not about the due process beforehand," he said. "They ultimately have to be found guilty of a crime." Once an offender has been convicted and sentenced, Hamadeh argued, that person should not be allowed to contact the victim or repeatedly summon the survivor back to court. "The victim shouldn’t be re-traumatized over and over again," he said. "At that point, they should have no ability to contact the victim ever in their lifetime." AOC OFFERS RARE PRAISE TO LATE SEN GRAHAM FOR BACKING AI PORN BILL NOW STALLED IN HOUSE Hamadeh said his time as a prosecutor showed him how emotionally punishing the court system can be for survivors forced to revisit deeply personal trauma. "You have to relive that over and over again," he said. "Justice is not complete if the victim still lives in fear," Hamadeh said. "Arizona already closed that gap. It is time the federal government did the same." The legislation now faces the Senate, where Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, is leading the effort to move it forward, according to Hamadeh. Hamadeh also credited Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz., for helping move the measure through the House Judiciary Committee and urged Americans to call on senators to bring it to the floor. "It passed unanimously in the House. It should pass unanimously in the Senate," Hamadeh said. "We should fix this once and for all and be able to save victims so much of this trauma and this terror." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hamadeh said he hopes the bill reaches President Donald Trump’s desk before November. "Call your senators," he said. "Ask them to bring up Kayleigh’s Law to the floor."

articles.title: Gloria Steinem, feminist writer and activist, dead at 92
articles.summary: Feminist writer and activist Gloria Steinem has died at the age of 92, according to a statement posted on her Instagram page Thursday.
articles.body: Feminist writer and activist Gloria Steinem has died at the age of 92, according to a statement posted on her Instagram page Thursday. "Yesterday, Gloria Steinem passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her," the message read. "Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end." "Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humor," the statement continued. The statement said Steinem "spent her recent years doing the two things she loved most: being in community with others and writing." "Gloria loved the tradition of lighting signal fires on hills to light the way to the other side of the mountain. Lighting your own candle for Gloria makes you part of this global and celestial community circle," it added. Born in Toledo, Ohio, in 1934, Steinem was a "founder of New York and Ms. magazines, and is the author of An Unexpected Life, The Truth Will Set You Free, But First It Will Piss You Off, My Life on the Road, Moving Beyond Words, Revolution from Within, and Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions, in addition to many collections and essays," a biography on her website said. "She co-founded the National Women’s Political Caucus, the Ms. Foundation for Women, the Free to Be Foundation, and the Women’s Media Center in the United States. As links to other countries, she helped found Equality Now, Donor Direct Action, and Direct Impact Africa," it added. "Among many tributes and honors for her activism, in 2013 she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Barack Obama and in 2019, she received the Freedom Award from the National Civil Rights Museum," the biography continued, noting that "Gloria’s home is the heart of Gloria’s Foundation and has become renowned as a magnetic and life-changing center for feminist and activist thinkers from around the world." Steinem "helped to found the Women's Action Alliance, a pioneering national information center that specialized in nonsexist, multiracial children's education, and the National Women's Political Caucus, a group that continues to work to advance the numbers of pro-equality women in elected and appointed office at a national and state level." "She also co-founded the Women's Media Center in 2004. She was president and co-founder of Voters for Choice, a pro-choice political action committee for twenty-five years, then with the Planned Parenthood Action Fund when it merged with VFC for the 2004 elections," her website said. Steinem began her career as a journalist, notably one who reported, in 1963, on degrading conditions in Hugh Hefner’s Playboy empire, an undercover assignment she came to later regret, according to The Associated Press. She credited a meeting six years later, where women spoke out boldly in favor of abortion rights, with changing her career path. "That speak-out was the beginning of activism for me," Steinem, who had undergone a secret illegal abortion herself at age 22, told the AP in an email in 2022, reflecting on the reversal of Roe v Wade. "Either our control over our own bodies is equal, regardless of sex or race, or we’re not living in a democracy." Well into her 80s, Steinem was traveling the globe and speaking out on issues of importance to her. These included everything from genital mutilation to Korean reconciliation, but it was equality for women that took precedence. "Being a feminist means that you see the world as whole instead of half," she once said. "It shouldn’t need a name, and one day it won’t." In 2020, her life was the subject of a feature film, "The Glorias, A Life on The Road," based on her 2015 memoir and starring Julianne Moore. And at 91, she collaborated on a picture book with Liberian peace activist and Nobel laureate Leymah Gbowee aimed at inspiring young people to change the world. "Rise, Girl, Rise: Our Sister-Friend Journey. Together for All" was published in February 2026. This is a developing story. Please check back for updates. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump’s Army secretary hunt takes shape as insiders float potential picks
articles.summary: Sean Parnell and Brian Mast are among names floated to replace Dan Driscoll as secretary of the Army after his reported clashes with Pete Hegseth.
articles.body: The hunt is on for the next secretary of the Army after Dan Driscoll submitted his resignation to the White House, opening a key leadership vacancy atop the nation’s largest military branch. Driscoll said Wednesday will be his "last full day" serving as Army secretary, adding that serving in the role under President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has been "the honor of a lifetime." The next Army secretary will inherit a service undergoing a major transformation, with questions over readiness and the Army’s role as the conflict with Iran continues. ARMY CUTS HELICOPTERS, PUSHES ‘AMAZON FOR WAR’ AS DRONE COMBAT RESHAPES MILITARY Army Undersecretary Mike Obadal could serve as acting secretary once Driscoll’s departure is finalized. A former special operations officer and defense industry executive, Obadal has also taken on a more public-facing role, including speaking at conferences. In the Trump administration, deputy officials have repeatedly stepped into top leadership roles after resignations or firings— including then-Navy Under Secretary Hung Cao becoming acting Navy secretary after John Phelan’s departure this year. Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman and a senior adviser to Hegseth, has emerged as one potential candidate, according to sources. PENTAGON FIRES BACK AFTER MARK KELLY ACCUSES PETE HEGSETH OF TARGETING WOMEN AND BLACK MILITARY OFFICERS "A lot of people inside [Office of the Secretary of War] want to see Sean Parnell become the next Secretary of the Army because they’ve worked alongside him and know what he brings to the table," a senior administration official told Fox News Digital. Parnell, who serves as assistant to the secretary of War for Public Affairs, is a former United States Army captain whose platoon killed over 350 enemy fighters at the height of the Afghan War. He unsuccessfully ran for the House in 2020 before launching a 2021 campaign for Pennsylvania’s open Senate seat, earning Trump’s endorsement. He later suspended his campaign amid domestic abuse allegations from his ex-wife, Laurie Snell, which he denied. HEGSETH TURNS TABLES ON DEMS AS SPARKS FLY DURING HEARING CLASH: 'I PUT THIS ON YOU' The senior administration official said Parnell understands the Pentagon and the problems inside from military experience paired with his work at the highest levels of the institution. "He also understands the importance of working alongside General LeNeve, who has been carrying an enormous load to keep the Army moving, and giving the Army Staff the leadership and support they need to get it back on track," the official said, referring to the acting Army chief of staff. A senior Pentagon official told Fox News Digital Parnell has "proven time and time again" that he is loyal to the president, citing that Parnell was present at his rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, where Trump was shot. After the president was removed from the rally, Parnell stayed behind to help others get out, the senior Pentagon official said. Parnell returned with Trump to Butler three months after the assassination attempt. "Their relationship goes back many, many, years at this point, and it's not just with the president. It's also very senior members of the White House that are with the President every single day," said the senior Pentagon official. REPUBLICANS DEFY JOHNSON TO ADVANCE DEMOCRAT-BACKED UKRAINE AID A third senior administration official told Fox News Digital that "Sean Parnell is 100% focused on the job he was appointed to by President Trump and Secretary Hegseth." Florida Rep. Brian Mast may also be under consideration, a source with knowledge told Fox News Digital. The Trump-endorsed candidate serves as chairman of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs and previously served in the Army for 12 years. Driscoll's exit comes after reportedly butting heads with Hegseth over concerns with the administration about the Army’s transformation and readiness, including his belief that Hegseth had hindered those efforts, Fox News Digital previously reported. Parnell defended Hegseth’s leadership and said the department remains united behind his vision. "Secretary Hegseth has been a transformative leader for the Department of War and, at President Trump’s direction, has ushered in a new era of Peace Through Strength. Standards and merit are back, our arsenal is stronger than ever before, and morale and recruitment across every service are at all-time highs," Parnell told Fox News Digital. "Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way." "The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first," he added. Democrats and some Republican lawmakers unloaded on Trump and Hegseth over the changes in the Department of War. North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said Hegseth is "creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks" while ranking Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee Jack Reed of Rhode Island said, "Hegseth is cultivating a culture where dissent is punished and competence is secondary to personal allegiance." Navy Secretary John Phelan was ousted in April after reportedly clashing with Hegseth over shipbuilding and management. FIRST ON FOX: TRUMP TO OPEN DIRECT LINE WITH MILITARY FAMILIES IN GROUND-UP READINESS PUSH CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The White House directed Fox News Digital to DOW when asked for comment. Fox News Digital reached out to Parnell, Mast, the Army and DOW for comment.

articles.title: Iran is no Vietnam, but Trump is mimicking Lyndon Johnson’s failed approach
articles.summary: Trump needs to learn the lesson in Iran that Johnson never did in Vietnam: that there is no slow squeezing of the enemy to the negotiating table.
articles.body:
President Trump and his national security team are heading back to the future in Vietnam.

No, we do not mean April 29, 1975, when the U.S. chaotically evacuated Saigon . Nor are we referring to the quagmire the Vietnam war had become by then.

Rather, we refer to Operation Rolling Thunder , which began in March 1965 and ended just after Halloween in 1968. The U.S. military’s limited aerial campaign was intended to coerce the North Vietnamese to the negotiating table. Instead, over time, it began planting the seeds that resulted in Hanoi’s victory over South Vietnam ten years later.

Today, Team Trump is attempting to wield a similar failed strategy in Iran. Like President Lyndon Johnson’s administration in 1965, Trump is trying to change Iran’s behavior without first militarily defeating it. As in Vietnam, it will not work.

Again, this is not to suggest Iran is a quagmire. But some parallels do hold. Both the Vietnam of 1965 and today’s Iran are using confusion over who is really in charge to keep Washington off-balance. Tehran is using this confusion to play for time. They see the upcoming November midterms as their best possible path to victory.

To that end, Trump, wittingly or not, is giving them the same time to pursue that strategy as Johnson gave the Vietnamese.

The parallels run even deeper than that. Trump, whether he realizes the historical and military parallels or not, is pursuing the same gradualist approach to war that ultimately felled Johnson’s strategy in Vietnam.

There is no slow squeezing of Iran to the negotiating table. Johnson, although he failed to learn from it, was first taught that when Operation Mayflower failed 71 days after Operation Rolling Thunder began in Vietnam. Johnson suspended Rolling Thunder for seven days in May 1965 as an incentive for Hanoi to come to the negotiating table. Instead, the North Vietnamese delegation in Moscow spurned him by refusing to receive then-U.S. Ambassador to Russia Foy Kohler’s offer to enter into peace talks.

Thereafter, for the next three years until 1968, Johnson kept trying to gradually coerce North Vietnam back to the negotiating table, much like Trump has been doing with intermittent cease-fires and bombings. It never worked, because airpower has limitations.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its leaders are creating their own modern-day version of the Vietnamese strategy against Johnson. Leaders in Tehran is more than willing to come to the negotiating table — the regime is even willing to sign deals, such as the June memorandum of understanding. But that won’t bind the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ commanders from attacking vessels attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz. They have no intention of honoring any deal the nation’s civilian leaders enter into with Trump’s White House.

Nonetheless, Trump keeps trying the same failed approach. By our count, U.S. Central Command has announced hitting largely the same type of target sets 16 times. Mowing the lawn, either as a strategy to bring Iran back to negotiations or to mitigate against attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, is not going to work.

Trump has failed to identify the decisive terrain in Iran. Likewise, Johnson never defined decisive terrain in Vietnam because he was not trying to win — he was just hoping to cut a deal with Hanoi.

Today, the Strait of Hormuz is the decisive terrain of the war and yet Trump refuses to fully secure it, opting instead to control it (doctrinally, there is a difference).

If Trump is to achieve victory in Iran, then he must stop micromanaging the war from the Oval Office. Johnson never learned that lesson. His Tuesday lunches with Secretary of State Dean Rusk and Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara, wherein strategies, targets, and tactics were decided, led to the quagmire that Vietnam eventually became.

Team Trump is not in a quagmire yet in Iran, but it must avoid repeating this same mistake.

Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. They are the cofounders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: GOP mail-in voting proposal could impact millions of Americans ahead of midterms
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's allies unveil a bill requiring mail-in ballots be received by Election Day, citing Florida's system as proof it works.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The nationwide battle over how and when Americans can vote has hit Capitol Hill, with two allies of President Donald Trump unveiling a new proposal they say will help restore confidence in U.S. elections. Rep. Laurel Lee, R-Fla., plans to introduce legislation on Thursday mandating that absentee and mail-in ballots are received by the relevant officials by the end of the day on Election Day. A corresponding bill is being led in the Senate by Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla. "This is something that we've done in Florida for many years, and it's a really effective way of making sure that elections stay organized and that we have timely election results," Lee told Fox News Digital. SUPREME COURT RULES ON MAIL-IN BALLOTS RECEIVED AFTER ELECTION DAY Lee is Florida's former top elections official, having served as its secretary of state from 2019 until May 2022. "Florida is proof-positive that this works, that it does not deny any voter the right to vote. Our job as elected officials or as elections officials throughout the states is just to make sure that voters know the deadlines, that they know the rules and tell them your ballot has to be received," Lee said. "They can do that just as easy as they can get it postmarked by Election Day." TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS It follows an executive order Trump issued in March 2025 essentially setting an Election Day deadline for when mail-in ballots can be received. If passed, the legislation could have a significant impact on millions of Americans, nearly a third of whom vote by mail. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FROM RESTRICTING MAIL-IN BALLOTS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS However, the topic of mail-in ballots has been a political lightning rod that's divided the GOP. Republicans in states where voting by mail is popular have expressed concern about changing the current system ahead of November. But Lee argued her bill does not curb people's ability to vote by mail. REPUBLICAN SAYS TRUMP'S TOP ELECTION PRIORITY 'DEAD' IN SENATE AS GOP FRACTURES AHEAD OF MIDTERMS "One thing that's important to understand about this bill is that it doesn't limit voting by mail. It simply says that for states who allow mail voting, ballots must be received by Election Day," she said. "So it still keeps all of those options that states have chosen to implement on the table for them. It just creates a different deadline." Meanwhile, a separate Trump order making significant changes to the mail-in voting system is currently at the center of a dramatic legal battle between the White House and over 20 states. That order would create new hurdles for the U.S. Postal Service and other agencies to verify proof of citizenship before delivering ballots, as well as mandate the use of specific stationery denoting federal election mail. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Supporters of the rule have argued it's key to enhancing voter confidence in elections, while opponents have said it would do the opposite by sowing chaos in the current system.

articles.title: 2028 Dem hopeful's longtime ally exposed for deep ties to CCP officials: 'Good friends'
articles.summary: Rep. Ro Khanna's, D-Calif. former senior advisor on foreign trade and economic development could be liability to a potential 2028 campaign due to his ties to CCP officials.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., has been floated as a potential 2028 Democratic contender for president, but his longtime ally and former senior advisor on foreign trade and economic development could be a liability due to his deep ties to Chinese Communist Party officials, a Fox News Digital investigation found. Henry Yin is a longtime California businessman and political operative who Khanna has praised for his "leadership" and has called one of his "good friends" on Facebook. He was born in China, raised in Taiwan and then moved to the United States, where he has lived for several decades. However, while living in California, Yin has been a major player helping China get a foothold in California over the last several decades through multiple roles, including serving as a member of the California Commission for Economic Development and founding a consulting firm that included multiple corporate clients with ties to Chinese Communist Party officials. A 2011 profile piece revealed that Yin "made his fortune selling used computer equipment to China" and had "done business in China for more than a quarter-century." The profile piece went on to say Yin has "good connections and a sense of [China's] business climate" and was "leading city trade delegations to China, which have contributed to several Chinese firms — most recently software company Trunkbow International — setting up offices in the city and helping city businessmen get a foothold in China." SWALWELL RESIGNATION COLLIDES WITH CHINA-LINKED SCANDAL AS CRITICS DEMAND FILE RELEASE "Henry has some sort of special skill-building relationships," one businessman said in the profile piece, praising Yin. "There’s a lot more government involvement in China, and you need relationships with local government officials." In addition to his consulting business and several overseas trips to China, Yin has allegedly attended at least 10 events hosted by United Front groups, including the All-China Federation of Returned Overseas Chinese (ACFROC), according to China expert Jackie Deal, the president of Long Term Strategy Group, a defense research firm. Fox News Digital has extensively reported on the CCP's United Front and the threat it poses to U.S. institutions as the CCP gains influence in the United States. In a Sept. 2019 Facebook post, Khanna announced that Yin, who was first appointed to the California Commission for Economic Development in 2010 by then- Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger and later reappointed to the position in 2015 by the succeeding Democratic Gov. Jerry Brown, would "serve as my Senior Advisor on Foreign Trade and Economic Development." "We discussed the importance of improving the US China relationship to cooperate on issues of climate change and medical research while protecting intellectual property and opening access to markets," Khanna continued. "I was particularly touched that Henry and the group had a birthday cake for me. It was wonderful celebrating with them!" A few months later, in December of the same year, Khanna posted about Yin on Facebook again, writing, "Thank you Henry Yin for your leadership!" That same month, Yin invited Khanna to be his "honorable guest" for an event titled, "S.V. U.S.-China Trading Partners Concerned Group Dinner Meeting Agenda," which was sponsored by Yin's consulting firm, USA-China-Link. A review of the event's presentations showed the attendees were slated to talk about an array of topics, including China investments, technology and business asset management, among other topics. Khanna was slated to discuss intellectual property. ELITE US COLLEGES LINKED TO CHINESE SURVEILLANCE LABS DRIVING UYGHUR ‘GENOCIDE,’ STUDY WARNS In Feb. 2020, Khanna posted another photo of himself having dinner with Yin, who he referred to as one of his "good friends." In the post, Khanna decried that "Chinese Americans are feeling they are being stereotyped as the symbols for the coronavirus." "This is a time to embrace our Chinese American neighbors and friends and continue to frequent Chinese-American stores, restaurants and shopping centers." On Yin's LinkedIn profile, which still includes the senior advisor title with Khanna's office, he includes over a dozen slides detailing his consulting business, USA-China-Link, and showcasing his business acumen in China, which was featured in several profile pieces in Chinese state media. One of the slides says his firm "specialized in high-tech and green tech" and helped China do business in California and vice versa. Other slides show a list of his Chinese clients and a slide that called him an "Official Commerce Rep in US for the Province of Fujian, China." Another slide shows a photo of Yin at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing in 2009 for the China National Day Banquet, where he calls himself a "VIP" in the caption. According to reports on the event, the banquet included several senior-level CCP officials in attendance, including then-Chinese President Hu Jintao and his successor Xi Jinping, the former third-ranking member of the CCP's Politburo Standing Committee, Wen Jiabao, among other top officials. A spokesperson for Khanna, who is a member of the House Select Committee on the CCP, told Fox News Digital earlier this year that "Henry Yin has never been employed by Rep. Khanna" and "he doesn’t serve in any role in his office or campaign." When asked Wednesday whether his office stands by the quote, Khanna's office did not immediately respond. Despite the previous denial, Khanna and Yin were pictured sitting beside each other earlier this year at an event. In Feb. 2026, Khanna posted a photo showing him sitting beside Yin at a political action committee meeting in Sunnyvale, California. Khanna wrote he was "honored to be back in the district, hearing directly from Chinese American community leaders." Yin has made several trips abroad to China over the last decade, including a July trip where he led a delegation to Guangzhou to meet with Zhu Xiaojun, the Department of Commerce of Guangdong Province's deputy director, which is a CCP-controlled position. A Chinese report on the trip said the two sides collaborated on two-way trade between California and the Guangdong province. Two months before the event, Yin attended the 2026 China-California Economic and Trade Forum, which was hosted by the Chinese Consulate in Los Angeles and included multiple CCP officials in attendance. He also accompanied California Gov. Gavin Newsom in late 2023 for a delegation, where he served as an advisor, according to another Chinese media report. During the trip, Newsom would meet with top CCP officials, including Chinese President Xi Jinping and Wang Yi, who has been a CCP member since 1981 and is currently serving as a "Member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, Director of the Office of the Central Commission for Foreign Affairs, and Minister of Foreign Affairs." Newsom also met with Han Zheng, China's vice president. A Fox News Digital review of Yin's Facebook account also unearthed other China trips he made, including Chinese delegations he has helped host in California. In 2014, Yin signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the California Green Tech Center and China Venture Capital Association, which appeared to be one of his firm's clients. Other posts show multiple China visits, including the 2015 "China South Asia Expo," which featured a speech from the now-former Chinese Vice President Li Yuanchao. A 2019 post highlights another China trip he took, which he called "fruitful" and included over a dozen photos of Chinese officials he met with. One of the photos included the names of Chinese and American companies where he was facilitating trade projects. ELITE US COLLEGES LINKED TO CHINESE SURVEILLANCE LABS DRIVING UYGHUR ‘GENOCIDE,’ STUDY WARNS A Fox News Digital investigation also unearthed a 2013 photo that appears to show Christine "Fang Fang" Fang — the Chinese spy at the center of the scandal involving disgraced former Rep. Eric Swalwell — alongside key political figures. Posing together at a public gathering, Fang stood behind then-Chinese Consul General to San Francisco Gao Zhansheng and top leaders from the Asian Pacific Islander American Public Affairs Association (APAPA), including Yin. A recently declassified FBI report on Swalwell's ties to Fang Fang revealed that a "prominent businessman in the Bay Area" tied to APAPA introduced Swalwell to Fang Fang. While Fox News Digital could not confirm whether the redacted section of the FBI report was referring to Yin, or potentially his brother, C.C., who founded APAPA and opened up several McDonald's franchises, Axios previously quoted Yin saying that Fang Fang was "very active" with the APAPA Bay Area chapter and remembered seeing her at several events. The photo was originally shared on Facebook in February 2013 by the late Don Sun, a prominent California civic leader and tech executive who passed away in 2024. In the photo caption, Sun wrote that the Yin family and APAPA had thrown a farewell dinner for the Chinese consul at San Francisco’s Embarcadero Center. Sun said the photo depicts the consul and "all my friends at APAPA." UNEARTHED PHOTO OF SWALWELL MEETING WITH TOP CCP OFFICIAL RAISES ALARM BELLS: 'VERY DISTURBING' An APAPA spokesperson confirmed that Yin is a current member of the group's board. The spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement earlier this year that the photo "appears to reflect a private gathering and does not represent APAPA programming, partnerships, or operations." They emphasized that attendance by individual members of APAPA at events "does not reflect organizational positions, affiliations, or activities beyond that context." "Public officials should strongly scrutinize any APAPA efforts that align with CCP objectives, including the CCP influence operations to prevent data center construction across America," Michael Lucci, the CEO of State Armor, a nonprofit countering CCP threats, told the New York Post. "APAPA does not have documentation to substantiate the characterization in Mr. Sun’s post that the dinner was ‘co-hosted’ by APAPA, and we cannot validate third party descriptions of the event based on a photo and a social media caption," the spokesperson said, adding, "Individuals may attend events in a personal capacity, and such attendance should not be construed as an organizational activity or endorsement." The spokesperson also noted that "APAPA has no records indicating that he [Yin] has served as a senior advisor to Rep. Khanna" despite an APAPA press release from January 2022 announcing Yin joining the group's national governing board and states that he "has served as Senior Advisor to U.S. Representative Ro Khanna, who represents the South Bay Area." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Pressed by Fox News Digital on this, the APAPA spokesperson said, "The current APAPA headquarters leadership and team had no knowledge of, and do not maintain any records confirming, Mr. Henry Yin serving as a senior advisor to Rep. Khanna. APAPA does not oversee, verify, or maintain records related to an individual’s outside titles or roles with public officials." They added that "With respect to historical references appearing on legacy APAPA web pages or posts, APAPA is in the process of reviewing and removing outdated or inaccurate content that does not reflect current leadership, governance, or verified records." They added that "questions regarding any past or current status with Rep. Khanna’s office should be directed to that office or to Mr. Yin directly." Yin did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

articles.title: How much can we believe the polls?
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ What to make of the polls ▪ Hegseth under rising scrutiny ▪ Google catches a break ▪ Schwartz’s first test as CDC director Most election observers seem to agree that about eight states are in play to decide control of the Senate this November. But looking at some recent polls, one might think solidly red…
articles.body:
Most election observers seem to agree that about eight states are in play to decide control of the Senate this November. But looking at some recent polls, one might think solidly red states like South Carolina and Arkansas are gettable for Democrats too.

Democrats have been riding high in recent weeks as they’ve developed a steady lead in the generic congressional ballot and are increasingly hopeful about flipping both the House and Senate on Election Day. They’ve also been boosted by President Trump ’s falling approval rating, reaching some of the lowest numbers he’s ever seen.

His approval rating currently stands at 39.4 percent in the Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) polling average , and some recent surveys have placed the number as low as the low 30s.

“I think anytime you see numbers this bad for an incumbent president ahead of a midterm election, it just bodes poorly for the president’s party,” said Geoffrey Skelley , the chief elections analyst for DDHQ.

The big question, though, is just how poorly it will bode this November. History is strongly on Democrats’ side in their battle to win control of the House, but the party is still fighting an uphill battle to win back the Senate. Or is it?

Polling has consistently shown a few states that Trump comfortably carried in 2024 have become key battlegrounds this year, including Texas, Ohio and Alaska.

If Democrats have a legitimate chance to flip those seats, that would suggest a much bluer national picture than 2024, one that most analysts agree is likely given the backlash the sitting president’s party often faces during midterm cycles.

But along with the polls showing Texas state Rep. James Talarico (D) a few points ahead in the Lone Star State and Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek (D) a few points behind in the Hawkeye State have been surveys suggesting Democratic candidates in ruby red areas are in striking distance, too.

In the aftermath of South Carolina’s GOP runoff last month, a pair of polls sponsored by Democratic nominee Annie Andrews ’s campaign showed her tied and leading by 3 points , respectively, against Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.). A poll from July sponsored by Democrat Hallie Shoffner ’s campaign showed her behind Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton (R) by just 3 points , while another poll not associated with any campaign found her leading by 3 points.

Similar results have been seen in certain House races. One released Tuesday sponsored by House Majority PAC, which works to elect Democrats to the House, showed Democrat Leela Gray leading Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) by 5 points in a district that Cook Political Report rates as “likely Republican.”

As Trump carried South Carolina by nearly 20 points and Arkansas by more than 30 points, these results create a somewhat hazier picture of what the electoral map actually looks like.

General distrust in polling has only increased following the revelation of a couple fake polls that were released this cycle and big primary polling misses in the Michigan Senate race and Wisconsin governor’s race.

Experts said the key is knowing how to read the polls and not making too much of any single result.

Generally, polls released by a campaign or sponsored by a partisan group are viewed with additional skepticism beyond independent public polling.

Charles Franklin , the director of the Marquette Law School Poll, said polls released by campaigns can provide useful data, but added that the public must keep in mind the motivations behind a poll’s release.

“A campaign only releases a poll if it serves their interest, if it advances their narrative, makes them look in better shape,” he said.

Franklin noted that past analyses have found campaign-sponsored polls tend to overestimate a result by about 5 points in their candidate’s favor. Even if that shift is implemented in some of the aforementioned polls, all of them would still be considered competitive.

Franklin advised against focusing too intently on a single poll, instead taking all polls on a race together to get an idea of where a race stands. If a poll, partisan or not, yields results significantly different from the rest of the surveys, that poll may be an outlier.

That may be the case in the Hendrix College poll that showed Cotton down by 3 points. (It was famously true of a poll showing then-Vice President Kamala Harris up 3 points in Iowa on Trump days before the 2024 election; she lost by 13 points.)

Roby Brock , the editor-in-chief of Talk Business & Politics, which sponsored the Arkansas poll, said in his analysis that although Trump’s approval rating appears to be affecting Republicans across the country, much can change ahead of Election Day, especially given Cotton’s sizeable financial advantage.

Franklin emphasized that despite the public’s eagerness to quickly react to a change, time is needed to confirm if it might be real.

“That’s frustrating for people who want to jump on the first hint of a movement, and say, ‘Aha! There’s suddenly been a change in the race,'” he said. “Now my advice is, wait a little while until you get more that convinces you that change is real. On the other hand, if you see something that’s unusual, pay attention to see if there’s other evidence that backs that up.”

▪ The Hill : Pro-Trump group releases first general election midterm ad.

▪ The Hill : Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) worried about losing majority.

Trump signed the short-term funding measure to keep the government open through Dec. 11 into law, officially preventing a possible shutdown before the midterms. The measure passed with overwhelming support in both houses of Congress.

Vice President Vance will take the podium today at 1 p.m. for the first White House press briefing in more than 40 days . It will also be the first press briefing since Karoline Leavitt left her post as press secretary one week ago.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s plane made an emergency landing at Reagan National Airport after the Coast Guard aircraft lost its right engine. All 14 people on board landed safely, and Mullin said the pilots “made the single engine landing feel routine.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth sits during a meeting with Australia’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence Richard Marles at the Pentagon, Sept. 2, 2026, in Washington. (Mark Schiefelbein, Associated Press)

DIRECT FIRE : Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is coming under heightened scrutiny amid the continued fallout from Army Secretary Dan Driscoll’ s resignation, which took effect at the end of the day on Wednesday.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), a lame-duck moderate who often bucks his party, stepped up his criticism of Hegseth’s leadership of the Pentagon on Wednesday and called on Trump to replace him as secretary.

Tillis noted he served for eight years on the Senate Armed Services Committee — including as the top Republican on the Personnel and Readiness subcommittee — and said he has “never witnessed more inept management” of the military.

“I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it,” Tillis wrote in a post on the social platform X.

Hegseth has ousted numerous key senior officials in recent months, including Gen. Randy George , who served as the Army’s chief of staff, and Christopher Donahue , the top U.S. Army commander in Europe.

Driscoll broke his silence late Tuesday, announcing that his resignation would take effect on Wednesday, but he did not provide a reason for his departure, instead saying, “i t has been the honor of a lifetime to serve.”

Other Republicans were critical of the shake-ups at the Pentagon, including Sen. Mike Rounds (S.D.), a senior member on the Senate Armed Services Committee, who said he was “disappointed” to learn of Driscoll’s resignation and expects his fellow senators to have questions for the Pentagon when they return from recess.

▪ The Hill : Hegseth headed for clash with GOP senators.

▪ CBS News : Military, civilian leaders who have fired or left under Hegseth.

LAND AHOY : The USS Abraham Lincoln docked at a port in Thailand on Wednesday after spending over 280 days at sea in the Middle East, a record-setting deployment.

The aircraft carrier’s arrival comes after reports emerged of a lack of food and hygiene products on board and worsening mental health among the sailors. Hegseth pushed back on those reports as misrepresenting the situation.

Pattaya, the seaside resort that has long been a landing spot for U.S. military, is trying to shake it’s reputation as a sex tourism hub.

Meanwhile, the recent military strikes exchanged between the U.S. and Iran are escalating as Tehran targeted U.S. allies and military bases around the Middle East early Wednesday.

Iran fired at U.S. assets in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan and Iraq in the hours after the U.S. struck multiple Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps sites.

Meanwhile, Trump floated renaming the Strait of Hormuz after himself on Wednesday, but later told reporters “that was just thrown out” when asked how seriously he was taking it. He previously suggested he would make the waterway a U.S. territory.

▪ Reuters : Trump aides seek ‘quiet’ in war.

▪ Politico : Iranian regime’s dynamics are fooling Trump.

KEEPING IT TOGETHER : A federal judge on Wednesday rejected the Department of Justice’s request to force Google to break up its advertising technology business after finding last year that the company had “willfully engaged in a series of anticompetitive acts” to gain “monopoly power” over the publisher and ad exchange markets.

U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema said Google does not have to sell off its AdX exchange business, which connects publishers selling ad space to online advertisers, nor does it have to open-source the technology behind its DoubleClick for Publishers platform or divest the business.

Brinkema still accepted “most of the parties’ proposed behavioral remedies, as modified by this Court,” though the details remain under seal. The Department of Justice’s antitrust division said it was “pleased that the court ordered substantial relief” and is “evaluating appropriate next steps.”

The case was the second major antitrust loss for Google after a separate judge ruled in August 2024 that the company had an illegal monopoly over online search.

▪ The Hill : New Jersey asks Supreme Court to review prediction market dispute.

▪ The Hill : Commerce secretary claims data centers ‘don’t use water.’

NARROWING MARGINS : The GOP’s majority in the House shrunk two days in a row as two Democratic House members were sworn in to fill seats vacated by one Democrat who died in office and another who resigned.

Rep. Everton Blair (D-Ga.) was sworn in on Tuesday after he won a special election to replace the late Rep. David Scott (D-Ga.), who died earlier this year. And Rep. Aisha Wahab (D-Calif.) was sworn in Wednesday following her special election win to replace former Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.), who stepped down in April amid sexual misconduct allegations.

Their additions narrow the Republican House majority to 218 Republicans to 214 Democrats, along with one independent who caucuses with the GOP. That allows Republicans to lose just two members on party-line votes presuming full attendance.

Both Blair and Wahab made history, as Blair is the first openly gay Black person to be elected to Congress from a southern state, while Wahab is the first Afghan American to serve in Congress.

The president will receive an intelligence briefing at 11 a.m. He will participate in signing time at 5 p.m.

Erica Schwartz testifies during a Senate Health Education Labor and Pensions committee confirmation hearing to be the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Capitol Hill, July 15, 2026, in Washington. (Mariam Zuhaib, Associated Press)

MEASLES DISCORD: Erica Schwartz is facing her first major test at the helm of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), as the federal agency finds itself in a highly unusual political disagreement with Pennsylvania after challenging two measles deaths reported by the state’s health department.

Schwartz was sworn in last month following a confirmation process in which senators grilled her about her willingness to push back against Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Schwartz has expressed strong support for childhood vaccines and pledged to “follow the science” in the new position.

But she has raised eyebrows in recent days after The New York Times reported that she personally ordered agency officials to challenge the two measles deaths in Pennsylvania, in a departure from the agency’s standard practice of accepting data provided by states.

“This week’s measles outbreaks update will not include the two measles-associated deaths reported by the Pennsylvania Department of Health on August 25,” the CDC wrote on its site, after Kennedy accused Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) of “manipulating” information.

The CDC does not list the number of measles deaths for 2026 in its tally, instead including an asterisk and attached statement about the Pennsylvania deaths, saying, “available information does not establish whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths or whether the individuals died from other causes while infected with measles.”

The Times reported that Schwartz ordered that statement be added to the site on Sunday.

Shapiro, during a press conference, said he spoke with Kennedy and “made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania.”

Amesh Adalja, an infectious disease physician at Johns Hopkins University Center for Health Security, told The Hill Insider that Shapiro has also gave a masterclass in how not to communicate during a public health crisis.

“Since the very announcement of these deaths, this has been run like a political operation rather than a public health operation, and these are the results you get,” Adalja told Nathaniel Weixel .

The heart of the controversy questions whether the deaths were caused by measles or whether the deaths coincided with the illness. One death was reported in a newborn and involved a ruptured spleen, while the second death’s details have not been publicly disclosed.

The Pennsylvania Health Department said both individuals were unvaccinated and tested positive for the measles virus.

A sign blaming Sacramento policies for high gas prices is displayed at a Chevron gas station in Alameda, Calif., on May 21, 2026. (Terry Chea, Associated Press)

DOUBLING UP : Chevron announced a deal Wednesday that would more than double its oil production in Venezuela — increasing it to more than 600,000 barrels a day.

The agreement is expected to be separate from the Trump administration’s announcement that it would partner with the Venezuelan oil company North American Blue Energy Partners, allowing it to gain access to more than 20 percent of the country’s oil reserves.

The Hill’s Rachel Frazin notes that it comes after the administration encouraged U.S. oil companies to operate in Venezuela. Chevron is the only major U.S. oil company that currently operates there, as ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips left in 2007.

Chevron said the increase will be done through a joint venture in which its subsidiary holds 49 percent interest. The venture plans to spend more than $7 billion over the next five years.

Chevron was assigned additional acres in Venezuela’s Orinoco Belt, where much of the country’s crude oil is found.

“Chevron’s history in Venezuela spans more than a century, and our expanded position reflects our confidence in the country’s deep resource potential and its ability to compete for investment within our portfolio for decades,” CEO Mike Wirth said in a statement.

Interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez said over the weekend that deals were also in the works with BP, Shell, Repsol and Eni.

articles.title: On the Ballot: The provocateur both parties can’t stop talking about
articles.summary: The name on everyone’s lips in Washington in one of the most talked about Senate races this fall is neither candidate. It’s Hasan Piker. He’s been described as a left-wing “streamer from California.” For some progressives, he’s part of the equation they argue the party needs to build a “winning coalition.” To other Democrats and many Republicans, he’s antisemitic and a “communist fanatic.” Piker, who boasts 3.1 million followers…
articles.body:
The name on everyone’s lips in Washington in one of the most talked about Senate races this fall is neither candidate. It’s Hasan Piker .

He’s been described as a left-wing “streamer from California.” For some progressives, he’s part of the equation they argue the party needs to build a “winning coalition.” To other Democrats and many Republicans, he’s antisemitic and a “communist fanatic.”

Piker, who boasts 3.1 million followers on live stream video platform Twitch, has become one of Republicans’ favorite talking points on the campaign trail — particularly in Michigan. Some Democrats argue the progressive commentator is a distraction from the high-stakes midterms while others view him as a threat to their party.

“I’m not going to defend … all of his views,” Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) told The Hill. “That’s for him to do.”

But “I don’t know why all of a sudden the standard is you have to agree with everything he said,” she added, noting lawmakers regularly work with colleagues they don’t share the same views with.

In the fierce fight for the open Senate seat in battleground Michigan, affordability, the U.S. trade war with Canada, data centers and health care have emerged as key issues. But the Los Angeles-based influencer has dominated the cable news shows and social media chatter.

“It is absolutely ludicrous that so much oxygen from sitting elected officials in the United States Congress is being dedicated to discourse around a Twitch streamer for young people,” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) told The Hill.

Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers has dubbed Piker, who joined Abdul El-Sayed on the trail during the primary, as the Democratic opponent’s “running mate” and pressed El-Sayed to disavow the far-left Twitch streamer’s controversial remarks.

Piker has been denounced for suggesting that Jewish people’s support for Israel could make antisemitism worse. He has also come under fire for his remarks on Hamas, the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks in Israel and 2019 comments stating, “America deserved 9/11.”

Piker has pushed back on accusations of antisemitism, saying his criticism is of the U.S. and Israeli governments. He acknowledged that he could have phrased his comments about 9/11 differently, apologizing to any he may have offended.

A spokesperson for Piker did not respond to The Hill’s requests for comment.

But it’s not just Republicans that have condemned the influencer. Many Democrats also want to draw a line in the sand.

Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.), a prominent critic of Piker’s, told The Hill that he “has engaged in a level of hate speech that has no place within our party — deeply anti-American sentiments that I think should be condemned roundly by everyone and not embraced by this party.”

“Not only should people not be on stage with him or take his support, they should condemn his views and what he has said,” Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.) echoed. “And I think anything short of that is unacceptable.”

While Piker is widely known as one of the most prominent Twitch streamers on the far left, his reach extends well beyond just one platform.

Bites of his livestreams — rapid fire commentary about politics and culture blended with real-time reactions to audience chats — are cut up and circulated everywhere from YouTube to TikTok, often getting picked up by media outlets like Fox News and MS Now, where commentators dissect his remarks.

“Here’s the structural problem with what I do as a livestreamer,” Piker told The New Republic in April .. “I’m talking for 10 hours a day on very volatile issues.”

“If you were talking for 10 hours a day, you’re going to say stuff that could very easily be misconstrued,” he added later.

Some argue that Democrats should be tapping into Piker’s audience, which is male-dominated.

“I think that we have been talking about how we need to reach out to all parts of our party, and also how difficult it is sometimes to get people to pay attention to politics, and so streamers are important in that,” Jayapal told The Hill, noting Piker isn’t the only online personality Democrats should court.

One of Piker’s first forays into the mainstream political sphere happened in 2020, when Ocasio-Cortez) and Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) played the video game “Among Us” popularized during the pandemic with Piker and other popular Twitch streamers in a push to turn out younger voters for the election. The stream garnered 400,000 views per Mother Jones .

In 2024, Piker attended the Democratic Natiional Convention as part of organizers’ push to reach younger voters via social media influencers. Piker was later kicked out of the convention, which he attributed to his criticism of organizers for not hosting a Palestinian American speaker. He initially backed Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) in 2020 before ultimately getting behind former President Biden that November.

He declined to endorse former Vice President Harris for the 2024 nomination.

That year election cycle male voters shifted to the right. And this demographic makes up much of Piker’s audience. Piker told Semafor in March that an average “Hasanabi head” is a white male in their mid-to-late 20s, noting that many have college degrees.

Piker gives fans “high level political analysis in a language that sounds like you might hear it across the bar,” Brandon Harris, a University of Alabama professor that studies creators and sports media, told The Hill.

A key part of his appeal, Harris explained, is his ability to tap into Gen Z and millennial angst over the economic instabilities facing their generation.

“They’re angry at not being represented, they’re angry at being told that their desires and political aspirations are childish,” Harris said. “And I think that, for many people, Hasan Piker is a cathartic experience.”

Yet, most Americans still don’t know who Piker is.

“I think the attention is way, way overstated. Over 80 percent of the voters do not know who he is,” said longtime Democratic pollster Celinda Lake , who’s working for El-Sayed’s campaign but spoke to The Hill her personal capacity. “And I think that a lot of conservatives are using it to divert attention from Trump.”

A June poll from The Economist/YouGov found that just 12 percent of respondents viewed Piker favorably while 66 percent did not know him. Sixty-eight percent of voters who cast ballots for the former vice president in 2024 also did not have a position on the streamer.

Younger generations — those between ages 18 and 29 as well as ages 30 to 44 — were more likely to know the streamer.

“I don’t know about all Democrats, but certainly for those of us who represent younger demographics, he does have a certain reach,” Omar, who has campaigned with Piker, told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins last month.

And Piker has only become more involved in the political scene in the last two years.

Piker was an early supporter of now-Mayor Zohran Mamdani ’s insurgent campaign in New York City. He also made national headlines in September of that year after the assassination of Charlie Kirk , the late conservative activist whom Piker was set to debate later that month. Piker wrote an op-ed for The New York Times condemning “the rising tide of political violence.”

Mamdani’s main opponent — former Gov. Andrew Cuomo ( D), who ran as an independent in the mayoral race— seized on Mamdani’s association with Piker. Ads paid for by a super PAC supporting Cuomo’s bid pointed to Piker’s 9/11 comments, NBC News reported . Piker has apologized for the remarks, which Mamdani called “reprehensible.”

These comments have defined the Twitch streamer on the national stage as he’s stepped up his campaigning for progressive and democratic socialist candidates this year — prompting some members of the Democratic Party to disavow him and urging their own to avoid appearing alongside him.

“He’s not a Democrat. He’s a Democratic socialist. So easy answer, no,” Scholten told The Hill when asked if Piker should play any role within the party.

Piker, however, has shrugged off the idea that he is a drag on his choice candidates.

“I think the fact that the Abdul race was so close meant that, you know, the fact that I was able to bring in the under 45 crowd early on and fundraising in key moments probably helped a lot in driving him across the finish line,” he told Vox earlier this month.

‘A liability’ with ‘potential political power’

Regardless, some Democrats worry that Piker has turned into distraction — a detriment to the party as they seek to flip the House and Senate this fall.

“[At] this point, he’s a liability because we can’t seem to talk about the issues facing Michigan, and how Abdul is a better candidate than Mike Rogers because the whole conversation is around Piker,” said Democratic strategist Antjuan Seawright .

articles.title: Trump urges Republicans in tight races to run on his record
articles.summary: President Trump on Wednesday urged Republicans facing tight races in the November midterm elections to run on his record, pledging to join them on the campaign trail. Trump told Republican lawmakers at a dinner in the White House Rose Garden that they had successful stories to pass along to voters in the remaining months of…
articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday urged Republicans facing tight races in the November midterm elections to run on his record, pledging to join them on the campaign trail.

Trump told Republican lawmakers at a dinner in the White House Rose Garden that they had successful stories to pass along to voters in the remaining months of the election cycle. In telling those, he said they will “win and you’re going to win big.”

“I’m going to go to every one of those 35 places, and we’re going to see if we can get everyone elected,” the president continued, referring to the 35 races that will determine GOP control of the House and the Senate in the fall.

Trump specifically referred to Senate races in Alaska and Texas. Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) who won the endorsement of former Anchorage Mayor Dan A. Sullivan, is slated to face off against former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) and Republican Dan J. Sullivan in the nonpartisan election in November.

In Texas, state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) is competing against state Rep. James Talarico (R) in a race to succeed Sen. John Cornyn (R), who Trump did not endorse in the GOP primary, favoring Paxton instead.

The president quipped about Paxton’s sense of style on Monday, saying that voters “might not love his look” but that he “was the best attorney general in the country, perhaps.”

Trump, who previously asked voters to act as though he were on the ballot , told Republicans Wednesday that there was “no reason for” them to lose the midterms based on his performance.

The president’s party typically loses control of at least one chamber of Congress following the midterm elections, in what is generally considered a referendum on their first two years in the White House.

Recent polling shows voters have grown dissatisfied with his job performance, with Reuters/Ipsos showing that Trump remains stuck at 33 percent , his lowest approval between his two terms. Another recent poll from the University of Massachusetts Amherst had his approval slightly lower at 32 percent.

The key factors in his low approval rating are his handling of the cost of living and the Iran war, the latter of which has caused energy prices to climb and impact inflation.

Trump is facing pressure not to let the conflict spiral after renewed strikes on the Iranian regime. The White House told Reuters that it would not escalate military action against Iran until after the midterms, but the president reiterated this week that he does not think the more than six-month conflict will last “much longer.”

“And I’m not affected by the election,” he told reporters Wednesday. “Number one, I’m not running, but my party’s running, and I’m going to help my party. But I think my party respects the fact that we’re not allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

articles.title: FIRST ON FOX: ‘No Kings’ protest network behind fight against AI data centers and Flock cameras
articles.summary: Fox News Digital traces how pro-China socialist groups moved from anti-Trump, anti-Israel protests into technology messages that spread to conservatives and libertarians.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The same hard-left network behind "No Kings" and other protests is leading the battle against data centers and Flock surveillance cameras, according to a Fox News Digital investigation and a new report. In growing protests from San Francisco to North Carolina, organizations and activists associated with the same ecosystem that rallied against President Donald Trump, Israel, Elon Musk, Tesla and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) over the last two years are now taking on data-center construction and license-plate readers. The overlap includes organizations funded by pro-China, Shanghai-based tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham, whose sprawling nonprofit and media network has faced Congressional and federal scrutiny over its funding and foreign ties. Singham and the nonprofits he has funded have denied taking orders from any government or political party and haven’t been charged with any crimes. INSIDE THE FAR-LEFT'S ANTI-DATA CENTER PUSH AND WHAT EXPERTS SAY IS DRIVING IT: 'PLAYBOOK WE'VE SEEN BEFORE' The findings are detailed in a new report, "The Compute War at Home," commissioned by Consumer Action for a Strong Economy, an Alexandria, Va., free-markets nonprofit that used social-media analysis by Arken Intelligence, a technology firm based in Washington, D.C., for parts of its study. "The money, media, organizing capacity and campaign objectives converge in the same ecosystem," the report says. Based on reporting over the past several years from street protests, Fox News Digital has identified the protest movement’s evolution across three phases. The new report chronicles a repeatable political model, in which activists first identify a local grievance, then connect it to a larger ideological narrative and package the argument through national media and activist infrastructure and carry it into new communities. The first phase appeared in early January 2025 with Trump’s inauguration and the launch of "Tesla Takedown" demonstrations to protest Tesla founder Musk as he led efforts to cut waste in federal spending. It became the mobilization infrastructure built around "No Kings" and "Hands Off" anti-Trump protests, anti-Israel activism and related campaigns, supporting the Communist Party of Cuba, the Islamic Republic of Iran and Venezuelan communist strongman Nicholas Maduro. Organizations from the Singham network – including the Party for Socialism and Liberation, CodePink, the People’s Forum, ANSWER Coalition and affiliated groups – appeared repeatedly across those movements, working with nonprofits more aligned with the Democratic Party, including Indivisible, a nonprofit network funded in part by billionaire Democratic megadonor George Soros. The organizations deny any wrongdoing as agents of alleged foreign influence and say they are addressing legitimate community grievances. AGITATORS UNITED BY CHINESE MONEY, HATE FOR AMERICA TARGET DATA CENTERS, EXPERTS WARN The second phase shifted that protest infrastructure toward American technological infrastructure. Over the past year, CodePink developed a national campaign against data centers, while the campaign took root among the approximately 70 chapters of the Party for Socialism and Liberation with near-identical messaging and strategies. Liberation News, which describes itself as the newspaper of the Party for Socialism and Liberation, nationalized local victories and promoted moratoria, bans and project cancellations. Media outlets, like BreathThrough News, from the Singham network provided additional amplification. The third phase involved an ideological crossover in which Flock cameras have now become a bridge between local privacy and policing concerns and the national fight over artificial intelligence, cloud systems, energy and data centers. The report doesn’t claim that every opponent of Flock cameras or data centers is connected to the activist network. It notes that opposition to Flock has become genuinely bipartisan, with legitimate concerns about privacy, data retention, misuse and poorly written government contracts. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis recently ordered license-plate readers removed from state highways, while Texas has also moved to pull back from the technology, and Republican Sen. Josh Hawley has launched an investigation into Flock cameras over surveillance concerns. But the report credits the left-wing organizers with fusing the two issues into a one-two punch that has caught on with a broad coalition. According to the Arken Intelligence analysis, posts mentioning both Flock and data centers increased from 639 posts in the 10 weeks before a spike in organizing on May 19 led to 9,009 posts over the next 10 weeks, a 14.1-fold increase. Among posts for which a political affiliation could be classified, the report said, 81% came from right-wing, conservative or libertarian accounts. "Issue pairings rarely multiply fourteen-fold in a matter of weeks without a catalyst, particularly when the surge begins immediately after organizers start promoting the connection," the report states. "These influence actions are cognitive warfare. Foreign actors don't need Americans to become pro-China," Rob Joyce, former director of cybersecurity at the National Security Agency, told Fox News Digital. "They need Americans to argue for the outcomes Beijing wants. And a free society that can't build the power and govern the advanced technology is going to wind up renting it from the adversary, read the PRC, that doesn't share its own values. And that scares me as an American." DOJ LAUNCHES GRAND JURY PROBE INTO MARXIST MOGUL NEVILLE ROY SINGHAM'S FUNDING OF LEFTIST GROUPS The report identifies at least a year of coordination among far-left activists in the Singham network, deliberately linking the issues through propaganda media outlets and activist networks funded and supported by Singham. Late last September, BreakThrough News laid the groundwork, publishing an article that described Flock as "America’s authoritarian tracking infrastructure." Soon after, People’s Dispatch, now merged into the BreakThrough News operations, covered a Denver campaign against data centers the next month, using a photograph from the Party for Socialism and Liberation’s Denver chapter and quoting a local Party for Socialism and Liberation organizer. By early May, the Party for Socialism and Liberation’s Denver chapter partnered with Indivisible and the far-left Sunrise Movement and promoted a forum examining the "connections between mass surveillance and data centers and how BOTH only serve the needs of billionaires and not our communities." PROBE INTO 'SUBVERSIVE' ANTI-AI SINGHAM NETWORK IS 'ENORMOUS,' FORMER TREASURY ADVISOR SAYS Days later, on May 19, when the convergence of issues went public, the local Denver chapter of the Party for Socialism and Liberation circulated a petition to urge the Denver city council to block the building of data centers, arguing, "FIGHTING BACK AGAINST DATA CENTERS MEANS FIGHTING FOR SOCIALISM!" It also posted photos opposing Flock cameras. On July 11, in Charlotte, N.C., the Party for Socialism and Liberation’s local chapter published an anti-Flock post centered on "AI mass surveillance" and police "brutality," then directed readers to sign a North Carolina petition opposing data-center construction on a dedicated website, nodatacentersnc.com, anonymously purchased the month earlier on June 19, according to online records. By July 25, In Tucson, Ariz., the local Party for Socialism and Liberation chapter joined "deFLOCK Tucson" and the "No Desert Data Center Coalition" for an event called "It’s ALL Connected" at the "Global Justice Center" on E. 26th Street. The promotional material asked what mass surveillance, data centers and electric power had in common. The answer: "IT’S ALL CONNECTED." The report says the campaigns combine concerns over water, electricity rates, land use, noise, health, immigration enforcement, policing and artificial intelligence. Those concerns can be legitimate, the report notes, but organizers can also use them to make the broader infrastructure supporting American computing appear inherently dangerous or illegitimate. In July, CodePink’s Detroit chapter published a description of data centers as the physical infrastructure of mass surveillance, linking them to OpenAI, Palantir Technologies, military contractors and ICE, crafting a narrative around the argument that the AI data center industry "creates harm and destruction." CodePink has dedicated a website page to a new campaign, "DATA CENTERS AND THE WAR ECONOMY," describing data centers as products and instruments of war and warning that projects "must be halted wherever they are." Its action page calls on activists to build a joint struggle against data centers and the "war economy." TEXAS GOV. GREG ABBOTT MOVES TO CUT STATE FUNDING FOR AI-POWERED FLOCK CAMERAS AMID PRIVACY CONCERNS Flock cameras provide a particularly effective local "entry grievances," according to the report. A dispute over a police contract, a license-plate reader or a single alleged misuse can be expanded into a broader argument about databases, artificial intelligence, cloud systems and data centers. "Flock gives that abstraction a visible local target," the report states, allowing organizers to portray "a much larger infrastructure buildout" as threatening. Flock’s actual computing footprint is small, according to company officials. According to Rahul Sidhu, chief strategy officer at Flock, the company uses less than 0.1% of the capacity of a single data center. But the report argues that Flock’s political value is far greater than its computational footprint because it gives the "surveillance state" argument a concrete and emotionally potent target. Ultimately, the causes have converged, say experts, with Republican politicians joining the chorus of criticism by pro-China communists in recent days against data centers and Flock cameras. As the Party for Socialism and Liberation continued to rail against "AI mass surveillance," DeSantis this week opposed the rise of an "AI digital surveillance state." The Senate Judiciary Committee previously asked the Justice Department and FBI to assess whether CodePink and the People’s Forum should register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, called FARA. The House Oversight Committee has sought records concerning Singham’s funding relationships, while the House Ways and Means Committee recently sent subpoenas to BreakThrough News, Tricontinental and the People’s Forum, which have refused to supply documents, saying they are the targets of a "witch hunt."
