articles.title: Mine safety commissioner fired by Trump gives up legal fight, citing Supreme Court
articles.summary: The Supreme Court’s expansion of President Trump’s firing power is sweeping into mine safety. Moshe Marvit, whom Trump sacked from the Federal Mine Safety and Health Review Commission (FMSHRC), moved to voluntarily drop his legal challenge on Wednesday. He disagrees with the high court’s decision but conceded it means the agency is no longer independent. “I brought this case to…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court’s expansion of President Trump’s firing power is sweeping into mine safety.

Moshe Marvit, whom Trump sacked from the Federal Mine Safety and Health Review Commission (FMSHRC), moved to voluntarily drop his legal challenge on Wednesday. He disagrees with the high court’s decision but conceded it means the agency is no longer independent.

“I brought this case to protect an institution that miners rely on, that can literally serve as the difference between life and death for mine workers,” Marvit said in a statement.

“I hope that future presidents and Congress will again make miner safety a priority and actively improve the condition of miners, rather than using miners as a political talking point while in fact making their working conditions less safe,” he added.

Marvit is among a growing list of fired independent agency leaders who’ve thrown in the towel after the Supreme Court upended 91 years of precedent that had shielded them with firing protections.

In June, the 6-3 conservative majority ruled in Trump v. Slaughter that the protections infringe on the president’s constitutional authority to fire them at will. It has enabled Trump to move ahead with his ambitions to carry out firings at independent agencies across the government, including ones that oversee labor disputes, product recalls, credit unions, air crash investigations and more.

Marvit served on the FMSHRC, which adjudicates safety enforcement and civil penalties when mine operators break the law.

He’s an attorney known for his writings on workers’ rights and was appointed to the commission by former President Biden. Marvit sued after one of Trump’s aides notified him in May that he was being fired.

“While the Commission still exists, it is no longer independent and is now — thanks to the President’s firing of me and the Supreme Court majority’s decision in Slaughter — subject to the political influence that Congress deliberately sought to avoid,” he said in his statement.

Marvit was represented by the law firm Katz Banks Kumin.

“Now with the fear of removal hanging over Commissioners’ heads if they decide against the president’s preferred outcome, the FMSHRC will no longer be a trusted arbiter of disputes between industry and miners — and miners’ safety will suffer,” Hugh Baran, one of Marvit’s attorneys, said in a statement.

“Make no mistake: more miners will die or be seriously injured on the job because of the Supreme Court majority’s decision in Slaughter,” Baran added.

Vice President Vance is set to hold the White House’s first press briefing in 42 days on Thursday afternoon, speaking in place of a press secretary — a role that remains vacant after Karoline Leavitt’s end-of-August departure . The briefing is set for 1 p.m. EDT.

The vice president was one of a handful of Trump officials who took the podium during Leavitt’s maternity leave, which began in late April. She returned in July but stepped down from the post last month to spend more time with her family, also transitioning to President Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc.

As of Thursday, the White House has not named Leavitt’s successor, though possible contenders reportedly include Anna Kelly, its principal deputy press secretary, and CNN conservative commentator Scott Jennings, among others.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries will hold a press conference at 10:30 a.m. EDT, after two members of the Democratic Caucus stung leadership on Tuesday by voting with Republicans on a procedural vote. The caucus met Wednesday to discuss the repercussions .

Meanwhile, the House is close to wrapping up its week. It passed a stopgap funding bill on Tuesday that had already made it through the Senate last month. President Trump signed the legislation on Wednesday, ensuring the government will be funded through the midterms until Dec. 11.

The House goes back on recess on Friday until its next session on Sept. 14, coinciding with the Senate.

Trump has no public events. He hosted vulnerable GOP candidates at the White House for a Rose Garden dinner on Wednesday, as the midterm elections kick into gear with Labor Day weekend.

articles.title: Andy Burnham praises UK-EU ties in meeting with Emmanuel Macron
articles.summary: The pair are discussing small boats, defence and Ukraine in Burnham's first bilateral talks in Downing Street.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has praised the UK-EU relationship as he holds talks with French President Emmanuel Macron about issues such as small boat crossings in the English Channel and defence.

The pair shook hands and posed for photographs alongside their wives outside 10 Downing Street on Thursday morning.

They are discussing "shared challenges" including the rise of "mega dinghies" crossing the Channel illegally, which the Conservatives say shows the UK government has failed to "smash the gangs".

Burnham said it was "so fitting" that Macron was his first overseas visitor in Downing Street since becoming PM in July, describing him as "our nearest neighbour and close friend Emmanuel".

"It shows what collaboration can achieve, just as we are also showing on Ukraine, on small boats, and also on strengthening the UK-EU relationship. So I look forward to discussing those themes further with you today," Burnham added.

Macron's visit to the UK was primarily to mark the Bayeux Tapestry's loan to the British Museum . The French leader met King Charles at the museum on Wednesday, ahead of the medieval tapestry going on public display next week.

In bilateral talks on Thursday, Burnham and Macron are discussing not just small boats but also the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as defence and EU co-operation.

But the "mega dinghies" crossing the Channel illegally - first seen earlier in August with a 15-metre long vessel carrying a record 230 migrants towards the UK - are arguably the most pressing challenge facing the pair.

It follows a summer when the overall number of small boat arrivals in the UK fell to a seven-year low.

Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.

Earlier on Tuesday, Home Office Minister Anna Turley said the officers were "just part of the armoury" of more than 1,000 officers on northern French beaches who are now doing "actual intervention" in the water.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that videos in recent weeks "show them going to the boats, slashing them, pushing people back, being bombarded with stones and bricks and coming under a lot of challenge to do that, so they are intervening".

In a post on X , in which he said he was "do[ing] politics differently", Burnham laid out the latest small boat, returns and asylum hotel figures, describing smuggling gangs as a "shared European challenge".

Asked about the extra police on French beaches, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch told the BBC she welcomed European collaboration "but the boats aren't stopping".

"We have spent hundreds of millions, if not billions, paying the French to man the borders," she said.

articles.title: Our healthcare system is crashing. Congress must stabilize it.
articles.summary: Congresswoman Maxine Dexter argues that the U.S. healthcare system is in crisis due to Medicaid cuts and corporate consolidation. She is calling for federal investment to treat healthcare delivery as essential national infrastructure.
articles.body:
When a patient is unstable and hemorrhaging, before we do anything else, we have to find a way to stop the bleeding and stabilize the patient. That is always the first step.

I spent more than two decades doing this as a pulmonary and critical care physician. Now, as a member of Congress, I am watching our healthcare system in freefall. Washington keeps responding as though there is time to spare. There is not.

Two forces are combining to push of our already-precarious healthcare system off a cliff. First, the Republican-controlled Congress and White House. Their multibillion-dollar cuts to Medicaid and their refusal to extend the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits have pushed more than 8 million people off their healthcare insurance. In Oregon’s 3rd District alone, an estimated 29,466 people could lose coverage. Second, the rapid consolidation of healthcare is placing more hospitals, physician practices, nursing homes, and community clinics under the control of large, profit-driven corporations.

These trends directly aggravate one another.

When Congress cuts Medicaid and chronically underinvests in affordable health coverage, clinicians lose essential revenue sources and are forced to care for more people with fewer resources. Some healthcare providers will close practices permanently, leaving communities without care. Others will be forced to sell to keep their doors open. Increasingly, those buyers are large, profit-driven healthcare corporations that view healthcare delivery as another stream of revenue. As independent providers disappear, local communities lose control over their healthcare, and patients are left navigating systems designed to maximize profit margins instead of meeting medical needs.

Consider Hahnemann University Hospital in Philadelphia, a 171-year-old institution that primarily served low-income patients and communities of color. In 2018, a private equity investor bought the hospital, failed to deliver on its promise to improve conditions, and closed less than two years later , selling the real estate for redevelopment. A registered nurse who had worked at Hahnemann for 17 years said the new owner seemed to have intended all along to buy the place, let it fail, and shut it down.

As a critical care physician, I know that a crisis rarely begins at the moment a patient arrives in the unit. By then, the warning signs have been building for hours, days, or years. The same is true of our healthcare system. If we wait too long to act, the damage will be impossible to reverse.

To stabilize the healthcare industry, we must treat healthcare delivery itself as essential national infrastructure. The interstate highway system was not built to maximize quarterly returns. It was built because the country understood reliable roads and bridges connect communities and expand opportunity. Their value cannot be measured solely by the revenue they generate or the returns they deliver to investors. We have never applied that same thinking to the places where our communities are born, healed, and cared for at the end of their lives. That is a profound failure.

The healthcare debate in Washington has rightly focused on expanding health insurance coverage to those who need it. That work must continue. But insurance is only meaningful if there is a clinician there to deliver care, a neighborhood clinic accepting new patients, a pharmacy that hasn’t closed its doors, and a healthcare workforce large and varied enough to meet the needs of the community. Preserving and expanding coverage must go hand-in-hand with stabilizing the places where people receive care and investing in the professionals who make that care possible.

For months, I have convened a healthcare working group of experts, physicians and advocates to develop a path forward. Our solutions are grounded in an idea that should not be radical: the delivery of healthcare is infrastructure, as critical as roads, bridges and clean water.

There is precedent for leveraging federal dollars to support critical healthcare infrastructure. In 1946, Congress passed legislation to fund hospital improvements because the country recognized access to care was a national priority, not merely a business opportunity. We should meet this moment with the same ambition. As financially strained hospitals and clinics seek lifelines, our goal cannot simply be to stabilize balance sheets so they can be absorbed by ever-larger healthcare conglomerates.

Public investment should preserve these institutions as community assets, with accountability to the people they serve rather than to investors. Today, public hospitals make up only 15 percent of the nation’s hospitals but a disproportionate share of our nation’s Level I trauma centers, often operating on tighter budgets than their private counterparts.

We are at a too-big-to-fail moment. Congress can continue to stand by, allowing private equity and corporations to buy up the healthcare system, with all the baggage that comes with their top priority being profits instead of patients. Or we can recognize healthcare is infrastructure and publicly invest in a system designed to serve people for generations. That is the choice before us.

In the intensive care unit, every second matters once a patient is crashing. As a country, we are past the point of pretending we have time to spare. Stop the bleeding and stabilize the system — then build it to last.

Maxine Dexter represents Oregon’s 3rd District in the U.S. House of Representatives.

articles.body:
Tech mogul Elon Musk’s super PAC has spent around $800,000 in top House and Senate races this cycle, according to the latest filings .

America PAC spent the most in Texas, doling out roughly $248,000 as Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton fights for the Senate in a toss-up contest against Democrat James Talarico.

The group spent around $170,000 in Maine, boosting incumbent Sen. Susan Collins (R) against Democrat Troy Jackson — and $106,000 in Ohio, where incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R) faces former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D).

The Republican Senate hopefuls in New Hampshire, Iowa, Michigan and Alaska also got a surge of funds.

The PAC put several thousand into eight high-stakes House races, supporting Republican Reps. Jen Kiggans (Va.), Tom Kean Jr. (N.J.), Mike Lawler (N.Y.), Ryan Mackenzie (Pa.), Scott Perry (Pa.), Rob Bresnahan (Pa.) and Derrick Van Orden (Wis.), along with Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer (R), who’s running for the House in Florida’s 25th District. They’re all in races that Cook Political Report considers toss-ups.

The new independent expenditures, which account just for the month of August, come after Musk reportedly met last week with Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) in Texas, where the party will be holding its first midterm convention next week to rally the base.

Musk — the world’s richest man with a staggering $916 billion net worth , according to Forbes — helped pour more than $250 million into President Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, but he said last year that he was planning to scale back his spending , which raised concerns among Republicans heading into a tough election year.

The Tesla and SpaceX CEO had helmed the Trump administration’s Department of Government Efficiency as Trump started his second term, implementing massive cuts and sweeping changes to the federal government. But his close relationship with Trump devolved in a public clash last year.

Tensions have since seemed to soothe , and Musk is jumping back into the political arena ahead of the 2026 midterms, with plans for his PAC to spend as much as $120 million on boosting conservative voter turnout.

articles.title: Democrats press DHS on election security funding

Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) and Rep. Joe Morelle (D-N.Y.) sent a letter to Mullin and Nick Anderson, acting director…
articles.body:
Two congressional Democrats are pressing Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin to “explain the delay as to why federal funds have not yet been provided” to local and state election officials for election security.

Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) and Rep. Joe Morelle (D-N.Y.) sent a letter to Mullin and Nick Anderson, acting director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), over “grave concern that time is running out” for the agencies “to assist state and local election officials in protecting our elections from cyber and mis- and disinformation threats.”

The lawmakers expressed frustration that it had been more than four months since DHS and CISA were given “clear, bipartisan instructions” to continue “Election Security Program activities funded in fiscal year 2024.”

This included failing to give funding for the continuation of the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center, also known as EI-ISAC, which “provided election security services to local election offices.”

“However, under your leadership, CISA has still not provided any of the over $39.6 million in appropriated funds to the EI-ISAC,” the pair wrote. “The failure to restore this funding as directed by Congress is a disservice to the thousands of election jurisdictions across this country.”

Padilla and Morelle also mentioned concern that CISA was “only just beginning to take steps to reestablish working relationships with election officials and rehire critical staff ahead of the 2026 midterms” after the agency lost hundreds of personnel .

“This is particularly disturbing at a time when our nation is at war with the Islamic Republic of Iran, which has reportedly engaged in sophisticated cybersecurity attacks,” they stated.

The Democrats referenced August attacks on local water systems in Minnesota, Michigan and New Jersey that resulted in “loss of monitoring and control functionality,” according to the FBI. CISA warned on July 22 of “ongoing Iranian-affiliated” cyberattacks on water facilities , days before the slew of attacks.

“Russia, China, and other foreign and non-state actors also have significant cyber and online election interference capabilities, which are likely increasing with advances in artificial intelligence technology,” the lawmakers wrote.

The lawmakers requested funding be distributed to the election analysis center and gave the leaders until Sept. 9 to respond to the letter “on the status of the disbursement of this funding and the hiring of critical election roles at CISA.”

articles.title: Dolly Parton kept cancer private to not ‘worry’ fans, niece says
articles.summary: Jada Star said Dolly Parton’s death has been “really difficult and very surreal” for the family.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Country music star Dolly Parton was thinking about her fans during her battle with cancer , according to her family.

The singer’s niece, Jada Star, said Parton kept her diagnosis “real private” because she didn’t want her fans concerned about her health.

“She never wanted to worry anybody,” Star told Extra on Tuesday. “So, I think it was just a shock.”

Parton died on Aug. 25 after a brief battle with cancer, her family revealed. She was 80.

Star said her aunt’s death has been “really difficult and very surreal” for the family, but the outpouring of love from the country legend’s fans has been “really bittersweet.”

“All of these tributes have helped so much to help us all through it,” Star, who is also a singer and songwriter, told Extra.

Parton’s family honored her wishes and laid her to rest at a private funeral at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in Nashville, Tenn., on Friday, Aug. 28.

Bryan Seaver, the “Jolene” singer’s nephew, revealed in the video announcing her death that Parton requested her final resting place be “comfortable.”

“Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy. He farmed the soil. She farmed songs and happiness,” Seaver said. “Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because after a life wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest.”

articles.title: Jeffries, Democrats shift tone, aim to move beyond defector scandal

Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) to back a GOP rule constituted “a significant breach of…
articles.body:
House Democrats appear ready to move beyond the defection scandal that riled the caucus earlier in the week.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and his top deputies had declared on Tuesday that the move by Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) to back a GOP rule constituted “a significant breach of trust” that demanded “a significant response.” Some Democrats were calling for them to lose committee posts.

On Thursday, however, Jeffries’s tone changed dramatically. The Democratic leader said he met with Gluesenkamp Perez, and the two came away agreeing to communicate “in a consistent way where we can arrive at shared priorities.”

“Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, of course, is an important member of the House Democratic Caucus fighting hard for the people that she represents in Washington and a leader of the Blue Dogs,” Jeffries told reporters in the Capitol. “And we value every single member in our caucus — progressives, the New Dems and Blue Dogs — and we’re going to move forward together, in unity, in order to solve problems for the American people.”

The change of tone reflects the reality facing Jeffries and his leadership team heading into the midterms. While those leaders want to send a message that going rogue on procedural rules won’t be tolerated, they also don’t want to harm one of their most vulnerable members politically just two months before the elections.

Gluesenkamp Perez represents a battleground district that President Trump won in 2024, and House Republicans have made her a top target in November.

Golden, who also represents a Trump-won district, is retiring at the end of this term.

Jeffries, who is in line to become Speaker if the House changes hands, also has an incentive not to alienate any members of the caucus ahead of the Speaker vote.

Jeffries said rank-and-file Democrats will continue to discuss potential changes to internal caucus rules in response to the defections, but he suggested there would be no punishments for the defectors, as some lawmakers had initially advocated for.

Jeffries said Gluesenkamp Perez spoke with Rep. Jim McGovern (Mass.), the senior Democrat on the Rules Committee, on Wednesday, and the two ”are going to resolve any differences that exist.”

“Because both of them — as is the case with the entirety of the House Democratic Caucus — understand what the stakes are in terms of defeating MAGA extremism in November,” Jeffries said, “and then as Democrats, getting off to a fast start in January.”

articles.title: Vance gives briefing room another whirl
articles.summary: ♀️ Plus: Rest in peace, Gloria Steinem {beacon} It’s Thursday. The deadlocked Lindsay Clancy jury is set to deliberate for the sixth day after it was unable to come to a unanimous decision on Wednesday. In today’s issue: Vance to hold White House press briefing The government is funded through the midterms Hegseth faces backlash Women weigh in on Gloria Steinem Programming note: We’re Abigail…
articles.body:
It’s Thursday. The deadlocked Lindsay Clancy jury is set to deliberate for the sixth day after it was unable to come to a unanimous decision on Wednesday.

Vance to hold White House press briefing

The government is funded through the midterms

Programming note : We’re Abigail Walker and Claire Leibowitz, filling in for Cate today. Please send me your tips, comments and story ideas to awalker@thehillcom or cleibowitz@thehill.com .

Vice President JD Vance will host Thursday’s White House press briefing, the first since July and since the departure of Karoline Leavitt last week.

The briefing, which will begin at 1 p.m. EDT, is the first in 42 days. Vance will act as placeholder for the still-vacant White House press secretary role.

It’s not clear what the vice president will discuss with reporters. But given this week’s headlines, the public might expect Vance to comment on the turmoil at the Pentagon , the latest developments in the Iran war or Republican strategy heading into the midterms.

GOP House leaders on Thursday cancelled two weeks of their September session, creating an abbreviated legislative schedule as the midterms approach.

The lower chamber was set to reconvene on Sept 14. but will remain out-of-office until mid-November.

Members could be called back should the Senate pass a budget reconciliation package.

Either way, they’ll now have plenty of time to campaign in their districts.

President Trump on Wednesday signed into law a stopgap government funding bill which will keep the government open until Dec. 11.

House Appropriations Committee Chair Tom Cole (R-Okla.) said on the House floor that while he didn’t approve of the entirety of the bill, he felt it necessary to avoid a shutdown ahead of the midterm elections.

“But they don’t really change the substance of the fact we bought the time that we need to get through the election cycle and hopefully the time that we need to get down to serious bargaining on the other side of it,” Cole said.

“It is not a good way to run our federal government,” Democrat Rep. Ted Lieu (Calif.) told reporters on Tuesday. “But it’s the only alternative that’s going to be before us, so I’ll be voting for it.”

Reporters asked Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) if he expects Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) to return by Sept. 14, the end of the Senate recess.

“I expect that. I sure hope so,” he said. “I have not talked to him personally, but I’ve talked to his staff regularly.”

The senator announced that he was discharged from a rehabilitation center in August after undergoing intense physical therapy to recover from a fall he suffered in June.

McConnell has not voted since June 11. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) in August said he had not heard from the senator after requesting updates on his health.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth quietly extended 50,000 troop deployments in the Middle East into next year, which could drag the conflict well beyond the quick fight he and President Trump promised over six months ago.

The deployment also includes 19 warships, air-defense units, fighter squadrons and paratroopers, the Journal reported, and is part of a strategy designed to give Trump options in the war, according to people familiar with the matter.

The administration is hoping economic pressure will eventually bring Tehran to the negotiating table, but it has been unsuccessful so far. The U.S. and Iran continue to exchange strikes.

Hegseth is taking fire from concerned GOP lawmakers over turnover from senior Pentagon staff, an unclear plan in Iran and the failure of the administration to reach across the aisle to Democrats.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), a former member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, on Wednesday blamed Hegseth for “inept management” of the Pentagon.

“He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force,” Tillis posted on social platform X.

Rep. Don Bacon , (R-Neb.) on Wednesday said he agreed with the senator. “I hate to tell the president who he should hire and fire,” he said on CNN’s “Anderson Cooper 360.”

“I wouldn’t hire him myself. He would not be on my team,” he added.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), a senior member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he was “disappointed” when he learned of former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll’s resignation.

And House Armed Services Committee Chair Mike Rogers (R-Ala.) told reporters Tuesday that he’s “tired of all the churn.”

💡 Why this matters: Hegseth may have to start answering questions if he wants Congress to pass emergency defense funding before the end of September to continue the Iran war.

Lawmakers are concerned over his lack of transparency, including over the USS Abraham Lincoln’s record-breaking deployment in the Middle East, as sailors spent over 260 days at sea. The aircraft carrier just reached Thailand on Wednesday.

Hegseth has largely ignored Democrats in pushing $70 billion in emergency funding. Some Senate Republicans say that’s a mistake.

Gloria Steinem , activist, author and co-founder of Ms. Magazine, died Wednesday at her home in New York City.

Despite her declining health, her wit and humor remained intact, AP News reports . She had recently written a memoir set for release this fall.

Women weigh in: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton joined CBS Mornings to share she was “heartsick,” calling Steinem an “architect” of women’s equality.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) took to the social platform X to say her advocacy helped “open doors once firmly closed to women.”

“May it be a comfort to all of us who loved Gloria that her extraordinary legacy will live on in every generation that carries her fight forward,” she added.

Lt. Gov. of Illinois and Senate candidate Juliana Stratton (D) said she was a “fierce leader, an unapologetic optimist, and a true hero,” on X.

Journalist Christiane Amanpour said Steinem “will go down in history as one of the most important activists of all time.”

And Stacey Abrams , former Democratic Georgia gubernatorial candidate, said the late activist “understood power: of women, words and coalitions, and she used that power to transform a stubborn nation.”

Trump on Wednesday urged Republicans in tight midterm races to run on his record, pledging to join them on the campaign trail.

Billionaire Leon Black filed a lawsuit Thursday challenging a House subpoena that demands he testify about his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Does Trump wear a wig? He said no during a speech at a White House Rose Garden dinner Wednesday night. He addressed the controversy and shared a story of bad weather and a bad hair day while speaking at a 2024 rally for Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio).

Associated Press : The Fed’s Waller says inflation report next week is pivotal in making the call on raising rates

NBC News : Man rescued from inside garbage truck in San Francisco

Politico : The far-right leader pushing Germans to forget the Nazi past

The New York Times : Can the Lindsay Clancy Jury Break Its Deadlock?

The House in and the Senate is out. President Trump is in Washington. (All times EDT)

1 p.m. Vice President Vance briefs reporters. 💻 Watch livestream

4 p.m. Trump participates in signing time.

🎳 Celebrate : Today is National U.S. Bowling League Day. Go hit the lanes!

🎂 Happy belated birthday, former NYC Mayor Eric Adams . The New York Post caught him in a “walk of shame” Wednesday morning after celebrating Tuesday night. Adams responded on X, “Hold on a second. Don’t you party all night on your birthday?”

🌳Bravo to “ Pablo Torre Finds Out,” which broke open the Kawhi Leonard salary cap scandal that resulted in major punishment announced Wednesday against the Los Angeles Clippers and it’s owner, Steve Ballmer . Some well-earned gloating on today’s episode .

Because you made it this far, here are two dogs, Alvin and Bear , chasing a giant black bear out of their yard in Montana.

articles.body:
Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) said Thursday that Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) is aiming to return to Capitol Hill from his months-long absence when the Senate reconvenes Sept. 14.

“I expect that. I sure hope so,” Comer told a reporter when asked whether McConnell would join his colleagues in the Senate when they return to Washington following the recess.

Though Comer conceded that he had not spoken to McConnell directly, the GOP representative confirmed he was in regular contact with the senator’s staff.

“They have all said it’s their goal for Sen. McConnell to be here when the Senate comes in next week,” he said.

McConnell, who hasn’t voted since June 11, was hospitalized on June 14 after a fall in his Capitol Hill townhouse. The 84-year-old senator announced last month that he had been discharged from the rehabilitation center where he was undergoing intense physical therapy as part of his recovery.

His prolonged absence has fueled questions about whether he will be able to return for the last months of his seventh and final Senate term. McConnell, who stepped down as Senate Republican leader last year, is not seeking reelection in November.

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) has publicly called for transparency around McConnell’s current health status, demanding the longtime senator show proof he is mentally and physically capable of carrying out the remainder of his term.

Several other GOP senators, however, have expressed their confidence that McConnell will return from his prolonged absence from Congress.

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) said McConnell was one of the “toughest guys I’ve ever met,” insisting that the Kentucky Republican is making progress and will be back.

Another fellow Republican, Sen. Joni Ernst (Iowa), said the letter from McConnell’s physician and updates to his colleagues in Congress were enough to explain his condition to the public.

Rep. Andy Barr (R-Ky.), who was endorsed by President Trump, will face off against Democratic nominee Charles Booker for McConnell’s reliably red Senate seat in Kentucky.

articles.body:
Fox News has parted ways with longtime anchor Maria Bartiromo, the network announced Thursday.

The network gave few details on what led to the host’s departure in a short statement that read “we thank Maria for her work over the last 12 1/2 years and wish her all the best on her next chapter.”

Bartiromo has been with Fox Business since 2014, and she emerged as one of President Trump’s most vocal supporters on the network during his time in the White House.

The host’s departure was abrupt, and the network said the final episode of “Mornings with Maria” aired Thursday morning. The show moving forward will be called “Mornings with Fox Business” beginning Friday and feature rotating anchors.

“Maria Bartiromo’s Wall Street” which also airs weekly on Fox Business will shift to “FBN’s Wall Street” effective this week hosted by Cheryl Casone and helmed by rotating anchors thereafter, the network said.

Bartiromo also hosted a weekend program — Sunday Morning Futures — which Fox pundit and former Rep. Jason Chaffetz (R-Utah) will anchor until a permanent host is announced at a later date.

A longtime financial news anchor and analyst, Bartiromo got her start in cable news as a producer for CNN. She later joined CNBC where she worked for two decades before joining Fox.

She has spoken glowingly on her various Fox shows about the president and his polices, regularly defending his economic and trade agenda.

Bottom line, we need to win,” Harris told host Peter Alexander on MS NOW’s “State of Play.” The former vice president…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris said Thursday she was not surprised by some red-state Democrats not wanting her endorsement, arguing those candidates are doing what it takes to win.

“We need to win, OK? Bottom line, we need to win,” Harris told host Peter Alexander on MS NOW’s “State of Play.”

The former vice president noted she has run in local, statewide and national elections, adding Democratic candidates this cycle “know what they need to do” to win their races.

“I would expect nothing less,” Harris remarked, adding she “is looking forward” to campaigning for Democrats where she can be “helpful.”

Multiple red-state Democrats have stiff-armed support from Harris in recent weeks, as the party seeks to take control of both chambers of Congress for the final two years of President Trump’s term.

Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek (D), running for Senate in the Hawkeye State, told reporters last week he did not want Harris to campaign for him.

The campaign of former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) also rejected support from the first female vice president after her PAC sent out a fundraising email for the Alaska Senate candidate last month.

Iowa State Auditor Rob Sand (D), who is running for governor , said last month he did not want Harris nor former President Biden to campaign for him.

“No thanks,” Sand told Politico’s Jonathan Martin . “Let’s move on. We need some new leadership.”

Sand also had no interest in Harris running for president again in 2028. When Martin asked him whether the former vice president should seek the Democratic nomination again, Sand replied, “Nope.”

Some Democrats, including Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.) and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, have welcomed support from Harris. El-Sayed said he was “grateful” to have the former vice president’s support after she endorsed him following his primary victory .

Harris, who dropped out of the 2020 presidential race before the primaries and lost to Trump in 2024, has not said whether she will run again in 2028. But she noted in April she “might” do so.

“I’m thinking about it,” Harris told the Rev. Al Sharpton at the National Action Network’s annual convention .

Harris is polling at or near the top of most recent national surveys of potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders.

But an August analysis from Sabato’s Crystal Ball noted Harris “performs particularly poorly in some state-level surveys,” including in New Hampshire — which is set to vote third in the next Democratic primary.

A survey of Granite State voters Saint Anselm College conducted on Aug. 17-18 found Harris in sixth place among a crowded field of Democrats, with just 3 percent support.

That put her behind former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.), Ossoff, Sen. Mark Kelly (Ariz.) and California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

articles.body:
Right-wing media personality Tucker Carlson described Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign as “literally Trumpian” in his podcast episode released Wednesday.

During an interview with conservative commentator Saagar Enjeti’s, the pair discussed the Michigan senate race between El-Sayed and his GOP opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.).

“I watch his campaign now, America First,” Enjeti said of El-Sayed. “When he talks about Israel, he says, ‘Israel is committing a genocide, but ultimately, I want to make sure that you don’t pay more for health care. I don’t want your tax dollars going abroad to fund this barbaric military.’”

“He stands in front of a giant American flag. It’s almost Trumpian in terms of a lot —,” Enjeti added, before Carlson cut in.

“Well, it’s literally Trumpian,” Carlson said.

El-Sayed, one of the many progressive insurgents that notched notable wins against more establishment figures in Democratic primaries this cycle, has pushed policies like the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Medicare for All and reduction of U.S. financial support for Israel.

Calls for the reduction in U.S. financial support to the Israeli government have grown in the last few years, especially in the wake of Israel’s war in Gaza — which has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians, destroyed infrastructure on a mass scale and resulted in a dire humanitarian crisis in the territory.

El-Sayed is also a critic of the U.S.’s war in Iran, which it has waged alongside Israel since February.

Trump has previously denounced long American wars in the Middle East. In February 2016, during a debate alongside Republican opponents, he went after former President George W. Bush for engaging in a war with Iraq — then calling the move “a big, fat mistake.”

In June, President Trump shot down the idea that he campaigned on not getting into “endless” wars.

“I didn’t promise anything. I don’t like these endless wars. This is not an endless war,” he told host Kristen Welker on NBC News’s “Meet the Press,” referring to the ongoing Iran war.

Carlson, a former Fox News pundit, previously supported President Trump — a stance for which he has expressed regret . The conservative media personality turned on the president after the Iran war began and even called for his removal Saturday due to speculation that Trump had considered using nuclear weapons in the conflict — which the White House has denied .

A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) official warned the agency about cutting corners in vetting officer candidates as the agency surged its hiring under the Trump administration.

The whistleblower report filed last August cited significant issues in how the department was reviewing its new hires, including making offers to candidates who had not yet passed background checks.

The filing asked the Office of Inspector General (OIG) for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to investigate the matter.

The New York Times on Thursday was the first to report the whistleblower report, filed by a high-ranking career ICE veteran who retired in July.

In the report, which was also obtained by The Hill, the whistleblower flags “systemic breakdowns in vetting.”

“This unprecedented lowering of standards sacrifices proper risk mitigation for expediency, placing DHS at risk of infiltration and insider compromise,” they wrote.

The whistleblower filing accuses the agency of ignoring “derogatory” information collected on candidates and even pointed to political appointees, saying they were able “to ‘jump’ agencies and secure law enforcement credentials.”

The concerns from the whistleblower come after lawmakers and other DHS officials raised alarms about the speedy hiring process.

Those have taken new urgency since the July killing of Joan Sebastian Guerrero, who was shot in Maine by ICE officer David Brouillette, who has faced a string of complaints, including from an ex-wife who had accused him of abusive behavior.

The OIG in August announced it would be reviewing ICE hiring and training.

DHS on Tuesday said it would not comment on matters regarding former personnel but defended its current hiring regime.

“The ICE Office of Professional Responsibility diligently applies the proper personnel vetting regulations, including guidelines for national security, and evaluates all available information for every applicant based on these factors,” DHS said in a statement.

“Applicants may receive a Tentative Selection Letter following their initial application and interview. Additionally, individuals may receive an offer of temporary status to begin training pending a full background investigation.”

Another DHS whistleblower testified before Congress in February, telling lawmakers that in condensing the timeline for training for new ICE officers, they were cutting significant material.

Ryan Schwank, a former lawyer for ICE, said training for new officers had been pared down to the point where it is “deficient, defective and broken” during a forum organized by congressional Democrats about “constitutional violations and abuses” within ICE policies. He accused ICE leaders of shielding training shortcuts from the public.

“For the last five months, I watched ICE dismantle the training program, cutting 240 hours of vital classes from a 584 hour program, classes that teach the Constitution, our legal system, firearms training, the use of force, lawful arrests, proper detention and the limits of officers’ authority,” Schwank told lawmakers.

Tuesday’s statement from DHS also referenced training standards.

“ICE training will now be extending to 72 days. The change, effective June 2, 2026, will apply to all new academy classes beginning July 1, 2026. All graduates of the previous academy curriculum will attend follow-on training at the Advanced Field Officer Training Program,” the agency said.
